beats.text: Look first at the goldsmith's hands. He holds a small pair of scales, and in the pan sits a single ring. A young, richly dressed couple watches him closely as he weighs it.
But now look at his eyes. They are not on the scales at all. They have turned upward, away from the work in his hand.
The room is a narrow workshop with three figures in it. In a round mirror beside the coins, two men on the street outside are looking in.
This man is no ordinary craftsman. He is Saint Eligius, patron saint of goldsmiths, and yet he wears a citizen's clothes, not a bishop's robes.
The panel is usually taken as a devotional picture that also served as an advertisement for the goldsmiths. So which is it, a prayer or a shop sign?

Why can we see into this shop at all? Look at the counter along the front edge, open to the street. Goldsmiths had to work in full view like this, so customers could check that nobody was doctoring the metal.

These rules came from the guilds of 14th-century Netherlandish towns, which curbed ruinous competition and guaranteed good work. One document of that time even forbade goldsmiths to attract custom by sneezing or sniffling.

Behind all this lay a fear of fraud. Countries used different units of weight and measure, so merchants weighed their goods with special care. In 1282 the Hanse merchants even had their own scales, built in Lübeck, set up in Bruges.
So it is probably no accident that the saint is shown weighing. Of all the tasks in a goldsmith's day, this is the one that rests on trust.

Now look at the round box on the counter, its lid lying open. The weights for his hand-scales were stacked inside one another and kept in it. And the hand that lifts them belongs to a very particular man.
Look again at the man behind the counter, at his citizen's clothes and the scales in his hand. His name was Eligius, born at Limoges around 588.
He became personal adviser to the Merovingian King Dagobert. A French children's song still has him telling the king his trousers are on back to front.
Legend has it the court gave him gold and jewels for one throne, and he made two. So the king named him minister and master of the mint.
Dagobert made him Bishop of Noyon, a diocese that included Bruges, where he founded three churches.
Some say he began as a goldsmith's apprentice, others as a blacksmith. The blacksmith story carries a miracle, a wild horse whose foot he cut off, shod and put back on.
He became patron of blacksmiths, goldsmiths and money changers, who shared one chapel and marched under the blacksmiths' banner.
Every guild had a patron saint, and a wealthy one had its own chapel. In citizen's clothes, the patron looks like one of the townspeople he protects.
In 1449, the year of this panel, the Chapel of Smiths was dedicated in Bruges. That may have been the occasion for the painting, though nothing proves it.
Look back at the scales. The ring in the pan is small, but it has been read in two different ways.
The first reading starts with an old legend. A ring said to have been made by Eligius for Saint Godeberta was once kept in the treasury of Noyon Cathedral.
In the story, rich suitors wanted to marry Godeberta, and the king had to give his consent. Eligius stepped in with his golden ring and declared her a bride of Christ.
So one reading sees the saint as a man who turns a girl away from worldly marriage. Another sees a guardian of marriage and of the wedding-ring trade, a profitable line for goldsmiths.
That second reading has objects on its side. A traditional wedding girdle lies on the counter in front of the couple. On the shelf sits a golden buckle that would fit it.

Now look at the couple themselves. She wears gold brocade with a pomegranate pattern, probably from Italy, and a gold bonnet embroidered with pearls. He wears a heavy gold chain and a brooch pinned to his bound headgear.

Only the Burgundian court or the richest burghers could dress like this. He may well have been one of the goldsmith's better customers. But nobody knows who they are, or whether they stand for a particular couple at all.
Now look at the coins lying on the counter beside the scales. There are gulden from Mainz and English angels. Beside them lie the heavy riders of Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy.

So how did so much foreign gold reach one counter? Bruges, then part of the Duchy of Burgundy, was the commercial capital of northern Europe. Furs and cod came from the north, silks and spices from the south.
On one day in 1457 its harbour held 42 British caravels and three Venetian galleys. Italian banks ran their northern branches here.
But the jewellers' best customer was the duke himself. Even his toothpick was solid gold, and at banquets guild goldsmiths guarded tables piled with his plate.
One salt cellar decorated with sirens was valued at about 900 ducats, roughly 200 years of a craftsman's wages.

The dukes travelled constantly with their treasure, and often paid for services in gold chains or jewelled boxes instead of money. So look again at the shelf of rings, silver pitchers, brooches and pearls, and at the heavy chain on the young man. This was wealth you could carry.
Look at the wall behind the saint. Small dark shapes like little trowels hang on thin gold chains.
They are probably adder's tongues, fossilized shark teeth believed to change colour when they touched poison. The two oblong pieces leaning on the wall were probably touchstones too.
Half hidden behind a curtain stands a goblet of coconut shell, a fruit thought to fight poison.
Princes feared poison with good reason. Philip the Good's father and uncle were both assassinated. In 1461 there was evidence of an attempt to poison his heir, Charles the Bold.
Rulers kept food tasters, and only ruling princes enjoyed the privilege of lids, dishes carried covered to the table.
Most things here were meant to protect as well as adorn. Branching coral was said to stop bleeding, rubies to fight putrefaction, sapphires to heal ulcers.
There is a rosary of coral and amber. The gold and glass vessel by the coral probably held relics or consecrated communion wafers.

In the early Middle Ages goldsmiths worked only for church and rulers. The most famous goldsmith of the 13th century was a monk. But not every object is a symbol, and some are simply painted with care.
Now move your eye past the coins to the small round mirror. Its curved glass holds red-brick Bruges houses and two men standing in the street.
They stand about where you stand now. So we see the shop from inside and outside at once.
Mirrors like this were common in Netherlandish homes, where one hung opposite a window brightened the room. Some called them witches, for their magic.
Look at the shelves behind the saint. Their angles suggest the painter did not know the new laws of perspective from Florence. He was still experimenting with space.
In the mirror, one of the two men holds a falcon. His head tilts in a way often seen in self-portraits.
Jan van Eyck painted such a mirror in his Arnolfini portrait, and it is presumed to hold his own reflection. So one reading sees a quotation here, and the falconer as Petrus Christus himself.
Falconry was a favourite pastime of the Burgundian court, with falcons imported from far and wide. But the sport was much too costly for a painter, who probably held a humble post at court.
The falconer's face stays uncertain, but the painter's name is easier to find.

Drop your eye to the bottom edge of the panel, where a line of Latin runs along it. Translated, it reads, Petrus Christus made me in the year 1449. Few painters of the time signed their pictures, and fewer dated them.
He was born at Baerle, probably in 1415. He became a citizen of Bruges on 6 July 1444. Seven years after joining a brotherhood in 1462, he was named a distinguished member of the painters' guild.
Beside the signature sits a small heart-shaped sign. It may be a master's mark, of a kind used in Bruges by miniaturists and goldsmiths, not painters.

So his training has been read in two ways. Some historians think he was a pupil of Jan van Eyck, completing works the master left at his death. Others think he trained as a miniaturist or a goldsmith.
The second reading would explain his bond with Eligius, and how exactly every object on these shelves is painted.
Look again at the shelf of silver pitchers, chains and brooches. Many such things had a short life.
After serving as payment, they were taken apart or recast. One goldsmith despaired so much that he left his trade for a monastery.
In 1476 Charles the Bold, the last duke, was defeated in Switzerland. His treasure fell to Swiss goatherds, who broke out the pearls and diamonds and melted the gold to sell it.
The guilds that kept this shop front open had helped Bruges rise. Then they became defenders of privilege, and their quarrels weakened the citizens' council.
By 1494 trade in Bruges had stopped, and 4000 to 5000 houses stood empty or ruined. Merchants and bankers moved to Antwerp.

The panel may have followed the money. A 19th-century German collector claimed he bought it from a Dutchman, the self-styled last member of Antwerp's goldsmiths' guild. Today it hangs in New York, a rare survivor of what it shows.
Come back, then, to the hands and the scales. The ring still sits in the pan, and the saint's eyes are still turned upward.
So, a prayer or a shop sign? As far as the evidence goes, it is both. Weighing is where trade meets trust, which is probably why the painter chose it.
In a play published in 1960 by Karol Wojtyla, later Pope John Paul II, a goldsmith speaks of his scales. My gold balance, he says, does not weigh metal but the life and lot of human beings.
